summary.text: The Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC) is the main current system in the Atlantic Ocean and part of the global thermohaline 'conveyor belt' that links the world's oceans.
Warm, salty water flows north near the surface, cools until it is dense enough to sink, and returns south as cold deep water.
Climate models predict it will weaken further this century, which would cool Scandinavia, Britain and Ireland and speed up sea level rise around North America.

facts.label: Deep water it forms
facts.value: North Atlantic Deep Water, mainly in Nordic Seas

facts.label: Southern upwelling
facts.value: About 80% of that deep water upwells in the Southern Ocean

facts.label: Recent strength
facts.value: Weaker by 2015 than before industrialisation, studies suggest

items.prompt: Warm, salty surface water travels north through the Atlantic and gradually cools. What happens to it?

options.label: It evaporates away completely
It freezes solid into sea ice
It grows denser and sinks
It gets lighter and spreads

items.explain: Cooling makes the salty water denser, so it sinks into the deep, an important part of what drives the circulation.

items.prompt: Water evaporates from both the Atlantic and the Pacific. What is the biggest reason the Atlantic ends up saltier?

options.label: Rivers carry extra salt into it
Winds carry its moisture off to rain on the Pacific
Salt leaks up from its seafloor
It is much shallower than the Pacific

items.explain: Trade winds carry Atlantic moisture across Central America to fall as rain on the Pacific, and mountain ranges stop it coming back, so salt builds up in the Atlantic.

items.prompt: Why can't Pacific surface water sink more than a few hundred meters?

options.label: Its seafloor is too shallow
Strong winds keep it stirred up
It is far too warm everywhere
Heavy rain keeps it too fresh

items.explain: The Pacific gets large amounts of fresh rainfall, so its surface water is not salty enough to sink very deep.

items.prompt: If the AMOC weakened, which region would see its average air temperatures drop?

options.label: Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia
Australia and New Zealand
The western coast of Africa
The southern tip of South America

items.explain: These regions are warmed by the North Atlantic Current, so weakening would lower their average air temperatures.

items.prompt: Scientists list a collapse of the AMOC as one of the climate's tipping points. What makes it one?

options.label: It happens every few centuries
It would only affect the tropics
Once collapsed, it would not recover
It would speed the circulation up

items.explain: A collapse would not be reversible, which is why it counts as a tipping point in the climate system.

items.prompt: Meltwater from Greenland's ice pours fresh water into the North Atlantic. What effect could this have on the AMOC?

options.label: Speed it up a lot
Have no effect at all
Reverse its direction
Help to weaken it

items.explain: Elevated flows of freshwater from melting Greenland ice are one way climate change may be weakening the AMOC.
